stages.title: Reading and writing fundamentals
stages.hook: Why does "teléfono" have an accent but "mesa" does not?
explain: Spanish stress has simple rules. Words that end in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the next-to-last syllable: me-sa, ha-blan, ca-sas. Words that end in other consonants are stressed on the last syllable: ha-blar, ciu-dad. A written accent (tilde) marks any word that breaks these rules: te-LÉ-fo-no, can-CIÓN.

Accents also separate words that sound alike: él (he) and el (the), sí (yes) and si (if), tú (you) and tu (your). Spelling is regular: b and v sound alike, h is silent, and c and g change before e and i.
stages.mnemonic: Break the rule, wear the tilde.
sentences: Yes, I live in the city.

gq.why: Words ending in s are stressed on the next-to-last syllable.

gq.q: What is the difference between "tú" and "tu"?
o: Tú means you; tu means your
gq.why: The tilde distinguishes the pronoun from the possessive.

panel.q: Why does "canción" need a written accent?
o: It ends in n but is stressed on the last syllable
panel.why: Words ending in n are normally stressed on the second-to-last syllable, so the exception must be marked.

panel.q: Which word is stressed on the last syllable without any written accent?
panel.why: Ciudad ends in d, so by rule the stress is on the last syllable.

panel.q: Why is the accent in "sí" important?
panel.model: The accent separates sí (yes) from si (if), which are different words.
panel.why: Diacritic accents mark different words.

teach.model: Look at the last letter. If it is a vowel, n or s, stress the next-to-last syllable. Otherwise stress the last. If a word does not follow this, it has a written accent.

stages.title: Basic sentence construction
stages.hook: "Yo tengo un perro" and "Tengo un perro" both work. Why can Spanish drop the subject?
explain: A basic Spanish sentence follows subject, verb, object: "María lee un libro." The verb ending shows the person, so the subject pronoun can be dropped: "Leo un libro."

To make a negative sentence put no before the verb: "No leo mucho." Adjectives usually come after the noun and agree with it: "una casa grande". The order is flexible for emphasis: "Come pan Juan" is possible, but the standard order is clearest.
stages.mnemonic: Put no before the verb: no hablo, no como.
sentences: They live in a big house.

gq.q: How do you make "Hablo inglés" negative?
gq.why: Put no directly before the verb.

gq.q: Where does the adjective usually go?
o: At the end of the sentence
gq.why: Descriptive adjectives normally follow the noun in Spanish.

panel.q: Why is "Hablo español" complete without "yo"?
panel.why: Verb endings show the person.

panel.q: Which sentence is correct?
panel.why: No goes before the verb. Unlike English, no helper verb is needed.

panel.q: Why is "Yo soy" sometimes said with the pronoun?
panel.model: The pronoun is added for emphasis or contrast, such as "Yo soy Ana, no ella."
panel.why: Subject pronouns mark emphasis.

teach.model: Put the doer, then the verb, then the object. You can leave out yo or tú because the verb ending shows who. Put no before the verb for a negative. Adjectives usually go after the noun.

points.ask: Can I leave out the subject?

stages.title: Common verbs
stages.hook: "Soy", "eres", "es": why does the verb "ser" look so different from "hablar"?
explain: Regular verbs follow patterns. For -ar verbs: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan. For -er: como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen. For -ir: vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven.

Very common verbs are irregular: ser (soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son), ir (voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van), tener (tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen). Stem-changing verbs like querer (quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren) change e to ie in the stem except for nosotros and vosotros.
stages.mnemonic: Boot verbs: the change stays in the boot, not at nosotros and vosotros.

gq.why: Ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van.

panel.q: Which is a stem-changing verb?
panel.why: Querer changes e to ie: quiero.

panel.q: Why is it "nosotros queremos" and not "queriemos"?
o: The stem change does not occur in nosotros and vosotros forms
panel.why: The stress falls on the ending in those forms, so no diphthong forms.

panel.q: How can you work out the verb form for "ellos" of "comer"?
panel.why: Regular conjugation.

teach.model: Take off the ending -ar, -er or -ir and add the ending for the person. Some verbs, like ser and ir, are irregular, so you must remember them. Boot verbs change the stem except for nosotros and vosotros.

points.ask: How do I make a regular verb?

stages.title: Nouns, pronouns and modifiers
stages.hook: Why is it "el problema" and "la mano" even though they break the -o/-a pattern?
explain: Nouns have gender, and articles and adjectives must agree. Most nouns in -o are masculine and in -a are feminine, but there are exceptions: el día, el mapa, el problema, la mano. Nouns ending in -ción, -dad are feminine: la canción, la ciudad.

Pronouns: yo, tú, él/ella/usted, nosotros/nosotras, vosotros/vosotras, ellos/ellas/ustedes. Possessives: mi, tu, su, nuestro. Adjectives agree in gender and number: "los niños altos", "las niñas altas". Plurals add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant: ciudad, ciudades.
stages.mnemonic: -ción and -dad are always feminine: la canción, la ciudad.

gq.why: Nouns ending in a consonant add -es.
Problema is masculine despite ending in -a.

panel.q: Choose the correct phrase.
panel.why: Article and adjective agree with the noun in gender and number.

panel.q: Which pronoun is formal "you" for one person?
panel.why: Usted is the formal singular you.

panel.q: Why do adjectives change form in Spanish?
panel.model: They agree with the noun they describe in gender and number.
panel.why: Concord.

teach.model: Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine. Articles and adjectives must match them. Add s or es for plural. Nouns ending in -ción and -dad are feminine.

points.ask: How do I make a plural?

stages.title: Questions and responses
stages.hook: In English you say "Do you speak Spanish?" What helper word is missing in Spanish?
explain: Spanish needs no helper verb: "¿Hablas español?" To ask yes/no questions, raise your voice or put the verb first. Question words have accents: ¿qué?, ¿quién?, ¿dónde?, ¿cuándo?, ¿cómo?, ¿por qué? Questions start with ¿ and end with ?
To answer, use "sí" or "no": "Sí, hablo español." For "why" use "porque" (because): "¿Por qué estudias? Porque me gusta." Remember: por qué (two words, why) and porque (one word, because).
stages.mnemonic: ¿Por qué? Porque. Two words ask, one word answers.
sentences: I study because I like it.

gq.q: Which is the correct way to ask "Why are you tired?"
gq.why: In a direct question, why is por qué.

gq.q: How do you answer a "why" question?
gq.why: The answer uses the single word porque.

panel.q: What is different in the punctuation of Spanish questions?
o: They start with ¿ and end with ?
panel.why: The opening mark shows the start of the question.

panel.q: "¿Cómo te llamas?" literally asks...
panel.why: It uses a reflexive verb: llamarse.

panel.q: How do you make a yes/no question in Spanish without a helper verb?
panel.model: You can use the same words as a statement and raise your voice, or put the verb before the subject.
panel.why: Questions use intonation or inversion.

teach.model: Start a question with ¿ and a question word like qué or dónde. You do not need do. Yes or no questions can just rise at the end. Answer with sí or no.

points.ask: Do I need a helper word?

stages.title: Describing people and places
stages.hook: Spanish has two verbs for "to be". When do you use "ser" and when "estar"?
explain: Ser is for identity and lasting traits: "Soy alta." "Es de Colombia." "La casa es grande." Estar is for location and states that can change: "Estoy cansada." "La casa está en la calle Sol." Compare: "Es aburrido" (he is boring) and "Está aburrido" (he is bored).
To describe a place, use hay (there is/there are): "Hay un parque cerca." Adjectives agree: "una ciudad bonita", "unos edificios altos". Comparisons use más ... que: "Mi hermano es más alto que yo."
stages.mnemonic: DOCTOR for ser, PLACE for estar.
sentences: The park is near the school.
There is a river in the city.

gq.q: Which verb is used for location?

gq.why: Profession is a lasting identity, so use ser.

panel.q: What is the difference between "Es aburrido" and "Está aburrido"?
o: Es: he is a boring person; está: he feels bored
panel.why: Ser gives a trait; estar gives a state.

panel.q: Which is correct for "The party is at my house"?
o: La fiesta es en mi casa.
La fiesta está en mi casa.
La fiesta hay en mi casa.
La fiesta tiene en mi casa.
panel.why: Events use ser for location: la fiesta es en mi casa; things use estar.

panel.q: Why is "La sopa está fría" better than "La sopa es fría" when the soup has cooled?
panel.model: Estar describes a temporary state or condition, such as soup that has cooled down.
panel.why: Estar for states.

teach.model: Use ser for who or what something is and for lasting traits. Use estar for where something is and for feelings that change. Use hay to say there is or there are.

points.ask: How do I say there is?

stages.title: Time, dates and daily routines
stages.hook: In Spain lunch is at 2 pm and dinner at 9 pm. How do you tell the time in Spanish?
explain: Time uses ser: "Es la una." "Son las dos." "Son las tres y media." "Son las cuatro menos cuarto." The question is "¿Qué hora es?" Days are lowercase: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. Months are also lowercase: enero, febrero, marzo.

The date is "el 5 de mayo". Daily routines use reflexive verbs: me levanto (I get up), me ducho (I shower), me acuesto (I go to bed). Habits use adverbs: siempre, a menudo, nunca. Meal times differ among countries: in Spain lunch is later than in many Latin American countries.
stages.mnemonic: Es la una, son las dos: one is singular, the rest plural.

gq.q: How do you say "It is 5 o'clock"?
gq.why: Use son las for hours after one.

gq.q: Are days of the week capitalised in Spanish?
gq.why: Days and months are written in lowercase.

panel.q: What does "Son las nueve menos cuarto" mean?
panel.why: Menos cuarto means a quarter to the hour.

panel.q: Why do many Latin American countries eat lunch earlier than in Spain?
o: Meal times vary by region and culture
panel.why: Customs differ by country, not by language.

panel.q: What do reflexive verbs like "me levanto" show?
panel.model: The subject does the action to itself, like getting oneself up.
panel.why: Reflexive verbs in routines.

teach.model: Use es la una for one o'clock and son las plus the number for others. Days and months are lowercase. Say el 5 de mayo for dates. Daily routines use reflexive verbs like me levanto.

points.ask: How do I tell the time?
How do I tell my routine?

stages.title: Food and shopping
stages.hook: At a Spanish-language market, how do you ask the price and say what you would like?
explain: To ask a price say "¿Cuánto cuesta?" or "¿Cuánto es?" To order say "Quiero..." or more politely "Quisiera..." or "Me gustaría..." Add "por favor". Say "La cuenta, por favor" in a restaurant.

Foods have gender: el pan, la leche, el queso, la manzana, el arroz. Food words vary by country: in Spain "patata", in Latin America "papa"; "aguacate" in Mexico, "palta" in Chile and Peru. Quantities: un kilo de, una botella de, un poco de.
stages.mnemonic: Quisiera = I would like: the polite choice.
sentences: I would like a kilo of rice.

gq.q: Which is the politest way to order?
gq.why: Quisiera is a polite conditional-style form.
In Spain it is patata; in Latin America, papa.

panel.q: Which is feminine?
panel.why: Leche is feminine.

panel.q: "Un poco de azúcar" means...
panel.why: Un poco de means a little of.

panel.q: Why might the same fruit have different names in Spain and Latin America or between Latin American countries?
panel.model: Spanish has regional vocabulary shaped by local history and by indigenous languages, so words differ across places.
panel.why: Lexical variation.

teach.model: Ask the price with ¿Cuánto cuesta? To order politely use quisiera and please. Food names have gender, so learn the article too. Some food words change from country to country.

points.ask: How do I ask the price?
Are food words the same everywhere?

stages.title: Everyday conversations
stages.hook: How do you speak politely to your teacher and casually to your friend in Spanish?
explain: Spanish has informal tú and formal usted. With a friend: "¿Cómo estás?" With a teacher or an older stranger: "¿Cómo está usted?" In many parts of Latin America ustedes is used for all plural "you", while Spain also has informal vosotros.

Useful phrases: "Perdón", "Con permiso" (excuse me when passing), "Lo siento" (I am sorry), "¿Me puede ayudar?", "Hasta luego". In Argentina and some other regions vos is used instead of tú: "vos tenés".
stages.mnemonic: Tú for friends, usted for respect.
sentences: Excuse me, can you help me?

gq.q: Which form do you use with a teacher?
Which phrase do you say when you pass between people?
gq.why: Con permiso is used to pass politely.

panel.q: Which pronoun is used for informal plural "you" in Spain?
panel.why: Vosotros is used in Spain; in Latin America ustedes is used.

panel.q: Where is "vos" widely used instead of tú?
o: Argentina and parts of Central America
panel.why: Voseo is common in Argentina, Uruguay and Central America.

panel.q: Why does Spanish distinguish tú and usted?
panel.model: It marks the relationship: familiar and informal with friends, respectful and formal with strangers or elders.
panel.why: T/V distinction.

teach.model: Use tú with friends and usted with teachers, elders and strangers. Say con permiso to pass, lo siento to apologise and hasta luego to say goodbye. Some regions use vos or ustedes.
